lesson.title: The Idea That Unifies All of Life
lesson.summary: Cell theory is the foundational idea that all living things are made of cells, that the cell is the basic unit of life, and that every cell comes from a cell that already existed.
lesson.body:
Cell theory rests on three simple statements that together explain what all living things have in common. First, every living organism is made of one or more cells. Second, the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life, meaning it is the smallest unit that can still carry out all the activities we associate with being alive. Third, all cells come from cells that already existed, rather than appearing from nonliving material. These three ideas together form the foundation that the rest of biology is built on, because no matter how different a bacterium, a mushroom, an oak tree, and a human being may look, all four are built from the same basic kind of unit.

This idea did not appear all at once, it developed gradually as microscopes improved. In 1665, Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork under an early microscope and saw a honeycomb of tiny empty compartments, which he named cells because they reminded him of the small rooms, or cells, in a monastery. Hooke was actually looking at the dead cell walls left behind in cork tissue, not living cells themselves, but the name stuck. Not long after, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek built more powerful microscopes and became the first person to observe living single-celled organisms swimming in pond water, which he called animalcules.

It took almost two more centuries for these observations to be turned into a general theory. In 1838, botanist Matthias Schleiden concluded that all plant tissues are made of cells, and in 1839, zoologist Theodor Schwann extended that same conclusion to animal tissues, together proposing that the cell is a universal building block of living things. Neither of them, however, had explained where new cells actually come from. That final piece was added in 1855 by Rudolf Virchow, who argued that cells can only arise from the division of preexisting cells, summarized in his own phrase omnis cellula e cellula, meaning every cell comes from a cell. This ruled out the older idea that living cells could spontaneously appear from nonliving matter.

Cell theory is powerful precisely because it applies without exception across the astonishing diversity of life. A single bacterium is a complete, independent living organism built from just one cell, capable on its own of growing, responding to its environment, and reproducing. A human being, by contrast, is built from trillions of cells, organized into specialized tissues and organs, yet every single one of those cells still arose through division from a preexisting cell, tracing all the way back to a single fertilized egg. That every organism, regardless of size or complexity, is built from this same basic unit is strong evidence that all life shares a common origin.

Because the cell is the smallest unit that can independently carry out the core processes of life, taking in and using energy, responding to its surroundings, and reproducing, understanding how cells are built and how they work is really the starting point for nearly everything else in biology, from how molecules like proteins and nucleic acids function inside a cell to how whole organisms grow, develop, and evolve.
